newsitem.title: UK: UK cabinet may discuss EMU, no policy change seen.
newsitem.headline: UK cabinet may discuss EMU, no policy change seen.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's cabinet may discuss a briefing paper on the European single currency this Thursday, officials said on Wednesday.

But Conservative members of parliament do not expect any major change in policy to emerge from the talks, particularly after media reports that Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind has swung behind the current "wait-and-see" policy.

A senior aide from Major's Downing Street office said on Wednesday he would not be surprised if the long-awaited paper, which media reports suggest has already been circulated to some ministers, was tabled at Thursday's cabinet meeting.

But he said it was still not confirmed and discussion of the Treasury paper, which was ordered before Christmas to look mainly at whether other European countries are "fudging" the criteria for entry into a single currency, could be postponed.

The paper was ordered before Christmas when Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke came under pressure from ministers who believe Major, facing an election by May, should take a more sceptical stance on the single currency.

Clarke is the most openly pro-European cabinet member. Media reports have suggested he threatened to resign if Major rules out entry into a single currency during the next parliament, a demand of Conservatives opposed to European integration.

But newspapers said Rifkind had now swung behind Clarke. The Daily Telegraph quoted what it said was one well-placed source saying: "Malcolm believes there are only two fundamental reasons for changing the policy, national interest or party interest.
"He feels that the national interest is well-served by existing policy and the party interest is not served by a change unless the cabinet is united."

The reports said Rifkind's move effectively ended speculation that Major could announce a hardening of his line on the single currency just before the election in a bid to catch out the opposition Labour party.
Government sources said the Treasury report, whenever it was discussed, was unlikely to change this.

Eurosceptics, Conservative MPs opposed to closer European integration, failed in an attempt to embarrass the government on Tuesday when they failed to force a parliamentary vote on their demands for a referendum over Britain's links with the EU.
The vote was intended to serve as a rallying point for those opposed to the government's European policy.

But the failure to force a vote, in part due to behind the scenes manoeuvering by Conservative party business managers in the House of Commons, defused one of the key potential flashpoints for the government over Europe.
